items.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
items.summary: One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.

items.title: Diamond laser system achieves 100% optical contrast in magnetic-field readout
items.summary: Researchers at Fraunhofer IAF have developed a laser-enhanced quantum sensor that combines high magnetic-field sensitivity with a large dynamic range. Using laser threshold magnetometry, they improved the ratio of sensitivity and dynamic range by a factor of up to 590 compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The breakthrough is enabled by the first demonstration of 100% optical contrast, combined with strong laser readout signals. The results, published in Nature Communications, open up new prospects for medical diagnostics, navigation, and resource exploration.

items.title: Sapphire-grown semiconductor film sets bandgap record
items.summary: Semiconductors with wider bandgaps could pave the way for smaller, more efficient electronics that can handle far higher voltages, but the wider this gap becomes, the harder it is to control how well a material conducts electricity. Now, a team led by Darrell Schlom at Cornell University has shown that adding silicon to thin films of aluminum gallium oxide can keep this control intact at bandgaps wider than any semiconductor before it. Their research has been published in Nature.

items.title: Embracing the glitches in gravity could give us a unified theory of reality
items.summary: Physicists have long struggled with their goal of making gravity a quantum force. A radical post-quantum approach might solve that problem – and clear up other cosmic mysteries, too
items.zh_full: 物理学家长期以来一直试图将引力纳入量子力学的框架，使其成为一种量子力。然而，这一目标至今尚未实现，引力与量子理论之间的鸿沟仍是物理学中的核心难题之一。本文提出，一种激进的“后量子”（post-quantum）思路或许能够解决这一问题，并有望同时澄清其他宇宙学谜题。文章认为，与其继续坚持将引力强行纳入现有量子框架，不如重新审视我们对引力的理解，甚至接受引力中存在的“缺陷”或“故障”（glitches），这些看似不协调的特征可能正是通向统一现实理论的关键线索。该观点挑战了传统量子引力研究路径，暗示未来的突破可能来自对现有理论框架的根本性反思，而非渐进式修补。
items.llm_summary: 本文讨论物理学家长期未能将引力纳入量子理论框架的困境，并提出一种激进的“后量子”思路可能解决该问题。文章认为，接受引力中存在的“缺陷”或“故障”或许正是通向统一现实理论的关键，这一观点挑战了传统量子引力研究路径，暗示未来突破可能来自对现有理论框架的根本性反思。
items.llm_reason: 探讨量子引力统一理论的新思路

items.title: Patterns of polar vortices discovered in lead-free superlattices on silicon
items.summary: A team at HZB has, for the first time, reported polar vortices in (BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃)₁₀ superlattices on silicon. These results expand the range of materials and substrates on which polar topological textures can occur and open up new options for incorporating complex ferroelectric states into silicon-based technologies.

items.title: 相比黑猩猩，人类为什么更容易患上骨关节炎？
items.summary: 一项基因组学研究表明，人类关节软骨中关键缓冲成分硫酸化糖胺聚糖（sGAG）的含量仅为黑猩猩等类人猿的约三分之一。这种在演化过程中出现的基因表达下调与软骨成分改变，虽然塑造了人类独特的骨骼形态，但也可能使人类更容易患上骨关节炎等退行性骨骼疾病。

items.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers
items.summary: Researchers at AIST have directly observed magnetic flux quanta generated in a superconductor by photon absorption and demonstrated a new principle of photon detection that identifies the number of photons based on the number of these flux quanta.

items.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
items.summary: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them.

items.title: What makes glass good at conducting heat? Sound holds the key
items.summary: Glass can keep a drink safely contained, protect a smartphone screen, or serve as a foundation for electronic components. But when it comes to controlling heat, this familiar material still holds some scientific mysteries. Now, researchers have identified a key factor governing how efficiently heat travels through silicate glass, offering a new guideline for designing glass materials for next-generation electronic devices.

items.title: Quantum interference traps electron waves in metal for first time
items.summary: Ever since quantum mechanics first described particles, like electrons, as rippling waves, researchers have wondered if those waves could be trapped in place. Writing today in Science a century later, a team of Columbia University researchers reports waves of electrons becoming trapped for the first time in a metal called Pd₅AlI₂.

items.title: Lost Schrödinger manuscript reveals his true view of quantum randomness
items.summary: Unlike classical physics, quantum mechanics generally cannot tell us exactly what will happen in an individual event. Instead, it predicts the probabilities of different outcomes. As one of the theory's early pioneers, Erwin Schrödinger played a key role in debates about what this randomness really means. However, part of his contribution has stayed hidden for more than 80 years.

items.title: Laser-made lattice reveals discrete light solitons in tunable atomic vapor
items.summary: Scientists from the Quantum Technologies Group at the Institute of Physics Zagreb, in collaboration with a colleague from the Physics Department at the Faculty of Science (PMF), have experimentally demonstrated for the first time the existence of discrete one-dimensional (1D) solitons in an optically induced photonic lattice in warm rubidium vapor.

items.title: Perovskite laser maintains stable performance over 400 million pulses
items.summary: In a study published in Advanced Optical Materials, researchers at Vilnius University (VU) demonstrated perovskite-based laser structures that maintained stable performance over more than 400 million pulses. Their findings address one of the major challenges limiting the practical use of perovskites: their instability. These semiconductor materials could play an important role in next-generation optical technologies, but their tendency to degrade has long posed a challenge for researchers worldwide.

items.title: 'Invisible' tweak could help make protein shakes less clumpy
items.summary: Scientists from RMIT University and Riga Technical University in Latvia have shown that static charge left on surfaces can be controlled, which may have big benefits for companies needing to avoid the little zap in production of common household goods. The discovery could even one day help stop powders such as protein, chocolate malt powders and coffee from clumping.

items.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about 10 seconds
items.summary: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices and allow them to exchange information encoded in the quantum states of particles, could enable more secure communications. To build these networks, physicists need to devise strategies that allow distant particles to share quantum states, preserving them long enough to perform calculations or enable communication between devices.

items.title: A hidden rivalry between two quantum states at the heart of superconductors
items.summary: Transmitting electricity without losing any energy may sound impossible, yet this is precisely the promise of superconductivity. For nearly 40 years, scientists have been working to understand materials that exhibit this remarkable property at relatively high temperatures. Unlocking their secrets could one day help make power grids more efficient, enhance medical technologies and support the development of quantum computing.

items.title: Oxygen collisions show evidence of jet quenching, a signature of early-universe matter
items.summary: New results from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) provide strong evidence that smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light generates a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a type of matter that existed just after the birth of the universe. The data, just published in Physical Review Letters, show that energetic jets of particles lose energy as they traverse the hot, dense matter left in the collision's wake.
